chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Muawiya ibn Wahb, who said:

I said to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him): Did the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) say: 'What is between my house and my pulpit is a garden from the gardens of Paradise?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Yes'.

And he (peace be upon him) said: 'The house of Ali and Fatima (peace be upon them) is between the house in which is the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) up to the door which faces the alleyway, up to Al-Baqi'. He said: 'So if you were to enter from that door, and the wall is in its place, it would hit your left shoulder.' Then he named the rest of the houses.
And he said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Prayer in my mosque equals a thousand prayers elsewhere, except for the Sacred Mosque, for it is superior.'

key_terms.رَوْضَةٌ: A garden or meadow, often used metaphorically for a blessed place in Paradise.
key_terms.مَسْجِدِي: My mosque (referring to the Prophet's Mosque in Medina).
key_terms.مِنْبَرِي: My pulpit (referring to the Prophet's pulpit).

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual significance of the space between the Prophet's house and his pulpit, and how does prayer there compare to other mosques?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi not only confirms the spiritual status of the space between the Prophet’s house and pulpit as a 'garden of Paradise' but also provides precise geographical markers for the residence of Ali and Fatima (peace be upon them), linking it to the Prophet’s sanctuary. It reinforces the concept of *Fazl al-Makan* (virtue of place) in Shia tradition, distinguishing the Prophet’s Mosque from the Sacred Mosque while elevating the domestic sphere of the Ahl al-Bayt as an extension of divine grace. The narration serves as a foundational text for understanding the physical and metaphysical layout of Medina during the Prophet’s era.
